evidence.text: The entry analyzes 蛋 as formed from 虫 with abbreviated phonetic 延, with animal egg as its basic sense. It says 蛋 is very late and absent from oracle bone and bronze inscriptions, Shuowen, and Guangyun; cites 字彙補 for both “蛋, anciently written 蜑” and the egg usage “俗呼鳥卵為蛋”; and gives egg examples from Journey to the West chapter 32 and Dream of the Red Chamber chapter 40. It describes later egg-shaped-object and abusive uses but supplies no dates for those extensions.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 蛋

evidence.text: The entry gives Shuowen xinfu’s analysis of 蜑 as 从虫、延聲 and glosses it as a southern ethnic group; notes it is absent from oracle bones and bronzes; cites Liu Zongyuan’s Tang-period prose for the ethnic-name sense and Su Shi’s Song poem for boat-dwelling residents; and cites Qing author Wu Zhenyu for 蜑 meaning chicken egg. It reports Guangyun’s fanqie 徒旱, upper tone, and the Shuowen xinfu gloss. It calls 蜑 an older form used interchangeably with 蛋 for eggs, citing 字彙補, but this does not establish that the egg sense was the original sense of 蜑.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 蜑

evidence.field: 延 early forms and graphic development
evidence.text: The 延 entry reports oracle-bone and early bronze forms as depicting a person walking on a road, analyzed as 彳 plus 止, with the sense ‘travel afar.’ It says 延’s form with 丿 appears in late Warring States Qin slips, and Shuowen analyzes 延 as 从㢟、丿聲. The entry treats 㢟/延 as an old/new form pair in classical texts and describes development of the 廴 element. This supports the history and sound of 延, not the naming of an object supposedly depicted in 蛋.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 延

evidence.text: In the Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese sound-series table, 蛋 and 蜑 occur under 延; the listed reconstruction variants across the series include *l'aːn, *l'aːnʔ, and *l'aːns. This supports a phonetic-series relationship, not by itself a claim about the egg word’s origin or the name of any depicted object.
evidence.title: 延 — 聲符 — 上古音系 — 韻典網

evidence.text: The Guangyun small rhyme 但 has fanqie 徒旱, voiced initial 定, 上聲, 寒 rhyme, open first division. The entry includes 蜑 among the characters in that rhyme. This provides a Middle Chinese comparison for 蜑 and its phonetic base, but does not give 蛋 its own Guangyun reading; CUHK states 蛋 itself is absent from Guangyun.
evidence.title: 但 — 小韻 — 廣韻 — 韻典網

evidence.text: Search results for this Zhengzhang Shangfang-based database record 蛋 as 声符 延, 元 rhyme, reconstructed *l'aːns, corresponding to Guangyun 憚. This is a database claim; direct page inspection failed due to a cache miss, so I treat the result as corroborating search evidence only. The independently opened 延-series page also places 蛋 in that series.

evidence.title: 蛋 — 字 — 上古音系 — 韻典網

evidence.source: 臺灣教育部《異體字字典》
evidence.field: dictionary status; recorded attestations and senses
evidence.text: The dictionary explicitly states 蛋 is not recorded as a headword in Shuowen. Its entry provides egg examples attributed to Guan Hanqing’s Yuan drama and Rulin Waishi; shape-like sense examples from late imperial works; insulting uses from Ming-Qing and later novels; and the southern coastal people sense, with a Song History quotation using 蛋丁. It documents varied senses but does not prove their chronological semantic derivation.
evidence.kind: government dictionary with cited textual examples
evidence.title: 教育部《異體字字典》— 蛋 A03630

evidence.source: 胡雲鳳, “說「蛋」,” 國立臺灣師範大學期刊資料庫
evidence.field: graphic history; egg-sense chronology; historiographic claim
evidence.text: The article abstract argues that Tang俗字 evidence shows 蛋’s graph arose through corruption/change from 蜑 around the Tang period; it separately dates the poultry-egg sense to about Northern Song, developing through Yuan and Ming and becoming established by Qing. This is a research conclusion visible in the abstract, not a directly inspected collation of the article’s cited examples.
evidence.title: 期刊論文 — 胡雲鳳〈說「蛋」〉

evidence.text: The opened text of 夢粱錄, volume 20, includes “三日，女家送冠花、彩段、鵝蛋” in a wedding custom description. This is a direct textual egg-use example in a work attributed to Wu Zimu and traditionally dated to the Southern Song, but the page itself does not establish the date or manuscript history. It shows the egg sense by the transmitted text, without establishing the graph’s formation chronology.
evidence.title: 夢粱錄/卷20 — 維基文庫

evidence.field: formation analysis; possible relation to 彈; readings
evidence.text: The entry presents a phono-semantic analysis with phonetic 延 and semantic 虫, describes 蜑 as a non-contracted form and 疋 as the current contracted graphic shape, and claims a late date based on absence from early corpora and dictionaries. It separately attributes the egg sense to 彈 (Middle Chinese danH, ‘pellet’) following Zhengzhang 2003. That loan/derivation proposal is distinct from the phonetic component analysis and is not established by the inspected primary sources. Modern readings listed include Mandarin dàn, Cantonese daan6, Japanese on タン and kun たまご, Korean tan/단.
evidence.title: 蛋 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: For 蛋 it records Mandarin dàn and Cantonese readings, while its graph entry has Guangyun status absent. For 延 it records Mandarin yán and Guangyun fanqie 以然, with a separate 去聲 reading 予線; it also displays Guangyun classification for 蜑 as 徒旱, 定 initial, 上聲, 寒/旱, open first division. Thus modern Mandarin 延 yán and 蛋 dàn differ, while the Zhengzhang Old Chinese reconstructions *lan/*lans and *l'aːns are similar within that system. Similarity is compatible with a sound component but does not by itself establish a particular borrowed lexical item.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 蛋; 延; 蜑 entries

evidence.text: The 蛋 entry displays Mandarin dàn. The 延 entry displays Mandarin yán and Guangyun fanqie 以然 for its level-tone reading, with a separate departing-tone reading 予線. Thus the modern Mandarin readings differ. In the Zhengzhang reconstruction cited by the phonetic-series entry, 延 *lan/*lans and 蛋 *l'aːns are similar within that system. This is compatible with a phonetic role, not proof of lexical borrowing.

gaps: 蛋 itself is absent from oracle bone, bronze, Shuowen, and Guangyun according to CUHK; no earlier direct graphic attestation for the 蛋 form was verified.
No glyph image was visually inspected. Descriptions of 延-to-疋 contraction or scribal confusion rely on lexicographic/article claims, not independent visual collation.

The claim that 蛋 arose from 蜑 through Tang-period graphic corruption is a scholarly account, but accessible material here was only an abstract and secondary excerpts; the precise dated manuscript/inscription evidence remains unchecked.

Sources conflict in formulation: modern graph analyses call 蛋 an abbreviated phonosemantic 延+虫 graph; the historical account treats it as contracted/altered 蜑, while the egg sense is later. Whether the egg use should be modeled as semantic extension of the ethnic-name graph, graphic borrowing, or influenced by 彈 (‘pellet’) remains unsettled.

Wiktionary’s proposed relation from 彈 (‘pellet’) to egg is not independently supported by inspected primary evidence; the source word, borrowing mechanism, and earliest attestations of both lexical uses were not established.

虫’s semantic contribution for 蛋 is a conventional classifier/radical analysis; the historical evidence does not establish that eggs were understood specifically as snakes’ eggs. The ‘snake egg’ gloss is a secondary assertion, not independently verified.

A secure earliest date for the egg sense remains unresolved. The opened 夢粱錄 text gives a Southern Song-attributed example; a scholarly abstract argues Northern Song onset; 字彙補 supplies an egg gloss but its compilation date was not verified in this research.
The precise semantic path from ‘egg’ to egg-shaped things and then abusive terms is not established by dated source sequence; dictionary gloss order is not chronology.

The ethnic group’s own endonym and recoverable historical pronunciation were not investigated. 延’s sound-series relation is independently supported, but that does not establish the origin or pronunciation of the ethnonym beyond the Chinese graph’s recorded phonology.

The opened sources do not provide a directly inspected individual Old Chinese 蛋 and 延 entry in one reconstruction table; Zhengzhang-style series data supports broad comparison, but reconstruction details remain dependent on secondary database presentation.
No Japanese-origin claim is supported; the Japanese readings are conventional Sino-Japanese/kun readings only.

No directly verified historical glyph image for 蛋 or 蜑 was found. The延 bronze SVG description page reports identity and reuse terms, but the page failed when opened and direct file URLs were inaccessible; it is not proposed as a downloadable candidate.
The Commons 卵 seal image is a modern redraw, not an artifact photograph, and depicts 卵 rather than 蛋; it is contextual only and is not proposed as a glyph candidate.

The detailed Tang graphic evidence underlying the proposed 蜑-to-蛋 corruption was not directly collated; only a scholarly abstract was inspected. The relation asserted there is chronological, but precise witnesses and variant shapes remain unchecked.

The source-word origin for the spoken egg word remains unsettled. A proposal relating 蛋 to 彈 (‘pellet’) appears in secondary material, but separate earliest attestations and a borrowing mechanism were not verified. A reconstruction of 蛋 does not establish the name or pronunciation of any depicted object; no such object-based borrowing is established here.
The semantic contribution of 虫 is a conventional component analysis. Evidence inspected does not establish a specific original referent such as snake eggs.

Earliest attested egg use remains uncertain: a scholarly abstract argues Northern Song onset, while CUHK cites a Southern Song-attributed text and later works. No independent chronology was reconstructed from those examples.
Dates and semantic links for egg-shaped senses and abusive uses are not demonstrated by the inspected dated examples; gloss order alone cannot establish chronology.
No Japanese-origin claim is supported. Japanese readings are conventional readings and do not establish Japanese formation.
No historical image was visually inspected; all image descriptions and reuse information are recorded as source descriptions only.
